profile.summary: The Plant Genomic Benchmark (PGB) is the set of eight supervised plant genomics tasks released with AgroNT, a DNA language model trained on 48 plant genomes. The tasks cover polyadenylation sites, splice sites, long non-coding RNA, promoter strength, terminator strength, chromatin accessibility, tissue-specific gene expression and an intergenic enhancer set, over 32 datasets in the paper's Table 1 (31 in the released dataset card's size table) with sequences from 101 to 6000 base pairs. It is for comparing deep learning methods on plant sequence prediction, in a field the authors say lacked a shared benchmark.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Introduction and Table 1. Dataset card: Dataset Overview

summary_quotes.text: Given the lack of comprehensive benchmarks in the context of deep learning-based methods in plant genomic research, we propose the use of the datasets covering several distinct genomic prediction tasks compiled here as the Plant Genomic Benchmark (PGB).
We present AgroNT, a foundational large language model trained on genomes from 48 plant species with a predominant focus on crop species.
This dataset features the 8 evaluation tasks presented in the AgroNT (A Foundational Large Language Model for Edible Plant Genomes) paper.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a model can predict functional annotations and quantitative measurements from plant DNA sequence. The eight tasks span regulatory features, RNA processing and gene expression: binary classification of polyadenylation sites, splice sites, long non-coding RNA and intergenic enhancer regions; regression on promoter and terminator strength; multi-label classification of chromatin accessibility; and multi-output regression of tissue-specific gene expression. The authors' stated aim is a shared assessment for deep learning methods in plant genomics, with attention to species that are little studied.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction, Table 1. Dataset card: Dataset Overview

quotes.text: We assessed the performance of AgroNT across several prediction tasks ranging from regulatory features, RNA processing, and gene expression
Our aim is to enhance and provide a comprehensive assessment of the performance of deep learning methods in plant genomic studies.
The tasks cover single output regression, multi output regression, binary classification, and multi-label classification

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Each task is a reuse or a rebuild of published data. Table 1 names the source of each: polyadenylation, lncRNA, gene expression and the enhancer set were compiled for this study, splice sites come from Baten et al., promoter strength from Jores et al., terminator strength from Gorjifard et al. and chromatin accessibility from Zhao et al. Polyadenylation sequences are 400 bp with the poly(A) site at position 301, and negatives were made by shifting that position by 1 to 50 bases, giving twice as many negatives as positives. The lncRNA negatives are mRNA sequences matched to each lncRNA on length and GC content. Promoter sequences are the 170 bp windows from -165 to +5 around annotated transcription start sites, measured by STARR-seq in two systems, tobacco leaves and maize protoplasts; terminators are 170 nucleotides from -150 to +20 around a cleavage and polyadenylation site, and the terminator study also added randomised sequences of varying GC content. For promoters, terminators and chromatin accessibility the authors downloaded the original studies' own train and test sets so their numbers can be compared with the original models.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is a fine-tuned model's predictions on each task's held-out test split, scored with the metric the task's source study used. The authors report AUROC and AUPRC for the imbalanced classification tasks (splice sites, polyadenylation, lncRNA, chromatin accessibility), the coefficient of determination R2 for promoter and terminator strength, and for gene expression the R2 of a linear model between predicted and observed levels on held-out genes. Fine-tuning in the paper uses IA3, which injects re-scaling vectors at the model's activations and updates about 1% of the parameters. The dataset card's size table gives the train, validation and test counts for each of the 31 datasets it lists; several tasks have no validation split, and the card notes that lncRNA fine-tuning was done on all six species datasets together because each is small.

sections.title: Promoter and terminator strength tasks
sections.body: These two tasks are regression on STARR-seq activity of 170 bp sequences from Arabidopsis thaliana, Zea mays and Sorghum bicolor, measured separately in tobacco leaves and in maize protoplasts, with terminator data covering Arabidopsis thaliana and Zea mays and over 50,000 terminators. The dataset card splits each task into a leaf and a protoplast dataset: 7154 and 7595 test sequences for promoter strength, 4806 and 4811 for terminator strength. The paper reports R2 of 0.7 in the maize system and 0.73 in the tobacco system for promoters, and 0.67 and 0.77 for terminators. Figure 3e and 3f compare AgroNT with the two CNN models from the original studies across plant species: on promoters AgroNT was ahead in every species and system, by 3 R2 points on average, and on terminators it matched or beat the CNN in 5 of 6 datasets.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The benchmark is distributed as a Hugging Face dataset with one configuration per dataset, loaded by name with the datasets library. The AgroNT weights are published separately on Hugging Face and through the InstaDeep nucleotide-transformer repository. No scoring script is published with the data, so the metrics have to be computed by the user, and the paper states that the pre-training code is proprietary and not released.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Eight tasks. Table 1 of the paper, and the summary table on the dataset card, list 32 datasets with six for gene expression; the dataset card's size table lists 31 datasets, with five gene expression datasets (Glycine max, Oryza sativa, Solanum lycopersicum, Zea mays, Arabidopsis thaliana). Table 1 gives the number of datasets per task: polyadenylation 6, splicing site 2, lncRNA 6, promoter strength 2, terminator strength 2, chromatin accessibility 7, gene expression 6, enhancer region 1. Sequence lengths run from 170 bp (promoters and terminators) and 398 to 400 bp (splice and poly(A) sites) to 1000 bp (chromatin accessibility and enhancers) and 6000 bp (gene expression), with lncRNA sequences from 101 to 6000 bp. Test counts per dataset range from 360 (lncRNA in cassava) to 377,873 (Arabidopsis donor splice sites).

facts.value: Fixed train, validation and test counts per dataset on the dataset card, with the split rule differing by task. Polyadenylation, splicing and lncRNA have no validation split on the card.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The models from the source studies, task by task: two CNN models for promoter and terminator strength (Figure 3e and 3f), the Zhao et al. chromatin accessibility predictions, and lncRNA-LSTM for the Zea mays lncRNA dataset of Meng et al., where AgroNT reached an AUC of 0.991 against the reported 0.9934. The paper also compares its gene expression results with two earlier models for Arabidopsis thaliana and Zea mays and reports up to a three-fold improvement.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Chromosome-level separation on the tasks the authors built: the polyadenylation and lncRNA test sets hold only sequences from one sampled chromosome per species, and the splice site test set is chromosome 5. Chromatin accessibility reuses the validation and test chromosomes of the source study. The lncRNA negatives are matched to the positives on length and GC content so that length alone cannot solve the task. No sequence identity cut-off between train and test is described, and nothing is said about overlap between the test sequences and the 48 genomes used for pre-training.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Polyadenylation site prediction, Splicing site prediction, lncRNA prediction, Chromatin profiles prediction

quotes.text: To prevent data leakage, we created a test set for each plant species that exclusively consisted of sequences derived from a single sampled chromosome.
To prevent data leakage, the test set was limited to chromosome 5.

To prevent the model from relying solely on sequence length for classification and to encourage the learning of more meaningful features, we performed a matching process between lncRNA and mRNA sequences based on both sequence length and GC content.

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Only for the lncRNA task. There the authors resampled the matched mRNA negatives five times per species and report the spread: the median range of the difference in AUROC across resamplings is 1.6 to 3.9 points and in AUPRC 2.5 to 4.6 points. No seeds, replicates or confidence intervals are described for the other tasks.

gaps: Table 1 gives six gene expression datasets while the dataset card lists five gene_exp datasets and the Methods describe five plants. The disagreement is unresolved by the sources read.
The dataset card's per-task test counts are not broken down by species for promoter and terminator strength, so the per-species results in Figure 3e and 3f cannot be matched to a test-set size.
Figures 3e, 3f and the other comparison panels print no numbers in the text; their values live in the figure data files in the Hugging Face repository, which were not fetched.
No source read states a licence for the benchmark's evaluation code, and the GitHub repository that distributes the model reports no recognised licence identifier.
The paper does not say whether the test sequences overlap the 48 genomes used for pre-training.

notes: Written from the PMC full text of the AgroNT paper (PMC11233511) and the benchmark's Hugging Face dataset card and API record at revision 78ec8156c2ffb3e5475277fdb7eb603294224e53. Points for a human. First, the paper calls the benchmark both the Plant Genomic Benchmark and the Plants Genomic Benchmark, including in Table 1's caption. Second, Table 1 says six gene expression datasets, while the card lists five gene_exp datasets and the Methods describe five plants, so the gene expression entry carries no dataset count. Third, the record's twelve stored protocols are per species within the promoter and terminator systems (A. thaliana, S. bicolor, Z. mays in maize protoplasts and tobacco leaves), but no source read prints a per-species test count: the card's counts are per system across species, so they are recorded here against the system-level datasets only, and the per-species values of Figure 3e and 3f live in the figure data files in the Hugging Face repository. Fourth, the leaf and protoplast dataset names are matched to the tobacco leaf and maize protoplast systems the Methods describe; the card itself does not spell that out. Fifth, where a task has several datasets with separate test counts, size is null rather than a sum. Sixth, the data are cc-by-nc-sa-4.0, so the dataset card bytes are not stored; the paper XML is CC BY 4.0 and is stored. Seventh, released is null on every entry: the Hugging Face API record gives only the repository's last-modified time (2024-06-02), which is not a release date, and no saved file states when the benchmark was released.
